reason: The rough edge must first break the skin and vessel before the bleeding can be stopped.
expectation: The body will receive a small cut, exposing the damaged vessel.

effect: The cut exposes a bleeding vessel that has already narrowed; platelets are the next likely defense.
reaction: The narrowing is a useful first response to notice.
reason: Platelets can gather at the damaged vessel to begin plugging the leak.
expectation: Platelets will collect at the cut and form an initial plug.

effect: The platelets formed a plug that slows the leak; clotting factors and fibrinogen may reinforce it.
reaction: The distinction between slowing and stopping the leak is useful.
reason: Activated clotting factors should convert soluble fibrinogen into fibrin for a stabilizing mesh.
expectation: Fibrin will form and become available to reinforce the platelet plug.

effect: Clotting factors converted fibrinogen into threads that can reinforce the platelet plug.
reaction: The mesh makes the reinforcement clear.
reason: Fibrin threads can stabilize the platelet plug at the damaged vessel.
expectation: A stabilized clot will stop the bleeding.

effect: The fibrin mesh stabilized the platelet plug and stopped bleeding, while the skin remained open.
reaction: The distinction between sealing the vessel and healing the skin is useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: Reinforcing the platelet plug was most worthwhile: the planned cutaway distinguishes stopped bleeding from a healed skin surface.

leastWorthwhile.text: Making the initial cut was necessary but predictable, with little explanation beyond the narrowed vessel.

surprise.text: The vessel was shown narrowing immediately after the cut, before platelets formed a plug.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the conversion from fibrinogen to fibrin glossed over how the clotting factors work.

continue.text: I would continue to see how the still-open skin repairs itself; the final picture leaves a clear next question.
